To accelerate the exploration of novel and efficient perovskite oxide-based OER catalysts, high- throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations have emerged as a promising alternative. Nevertheless, these calcula- tions often require prior knowledge of specificalgorithmsor methods, hindering data unification across different systems and limiting the universal applicability of the results under various conditions⁹. Additionally, while computational costs are lower than experimental work, they are not negligible, further compli- cating seamless plug-and-play implementation. Recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have unveiled its remarkable potential in the discovery of novel electrocatalysts¹⁰. Machine learning (ML) offers a data-driven methodology for extracting quantitative composition-catalytic property relationships, holding the promise to expedite materials design by orders of magnitude 11,12. The majority of data inputs for ML models typically stem from published experimental data/open-source databases, serving as a cornerstone for the generation of derivative new candidates 13,14. Some efforts have focused on using ML to identify highly relevant descriptors, thereby simplifying the system and accelerating the prediction process 15–17. However, the ML algorithms based on feature selection and simplification often eliminate less- significant descriptors, inevitably leading to information loss and diminished prediction accuracy. Moreover, when analyzing the relative importance of the same dataset, different algorithms fre- quently produce inconsistent results¹⁸. Consequently, the reliability of feature importance interpretations in the absence of domain expertise is often questionable 19,20. In addition to the choice of algorithms, the quality and quantity of data play a crucial role in determining the accuracy of ML-based pre- dictions. Conventional simulation databases derived from DFT are often limited to a single or a few similar systems, restricting the range of applicability and generalizability of the extracted knowledge. Moreover, experimental data, while valuable, are relatively scarce and challenging to consolidate due to the lack of universally accepted standards for reporting experimental methodologies. Despite recent advancements in unifying inconsistently reported data from diverse sources, these efforts remain limited to specificreactionsandoften involve feature selection, resulting in trimmed feature sets that may exclude potentially valuable information²¹. To tackle this challenge, herein, we propose a powerful transfer learning paradigm centered on the cation information of perovskite oxide electrocatalysts. This approach leverages pre-trained models to effectively integrate OER data with vast datasets from diverse research fields, encompassing a broader range of perovskite compositions. Additionally, we employ ensemble methodologies to combine models derived from distinct sub-clusters identified through a com- bination of domain knowledge and unsupervised learning techniques. This strategy facilitates the transfer of knowledge across diverse material systems, leading to a significant improvement in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the incorporation of active learning metho- dology expands the predictive capabilities to more complex hexanary material systems, extending beyond the initial focus on quinary sys- tems. The Pr0.1Sr0.9Co0.5Fe0.5O₃ (PSCF) and Pr0.1Sr0.9Co0.5Fe0.3Mn0.2O₃ (PSCFM) demonstrated remarkable OER activity, with low over- potentials below 330 mV (at 10 mA cm −2 in 1 M KOH). Comprehensive characterizations reveal that lattice oxygen plays a key role in facil- itating O-O coupling during the OER process. DFT calculations further elucidate the mechanistic underpinnings of this enhanced OER activ- ity. The incorporation of Mn into PSCF strengthens the stability of Co reactive sites, while simultaneously lowering the reaction barrier through the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM) pathway on Mn-O-Co motifs. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of transfer learning and active learning in overcoming data limitations and achieving accurate prediction of OER catalysts.

Leveraging polyphyletic data sources, we established a transfer ML framework that exhibits enhanced generalization capabilities for the precise estimation of a family of non-noble-metal perovskite oxide electrocatalysts for alkaline OER. Notably, the PSCF and PSCFM electrocatalysts exhibited low overpotentials of 327 mV and 315 mV at 10 mA cm −2, respectively. A comprehensive suite of in situ/operando characterization techniques revealed that both AEM and LOM path- ways operate on the electrocatalysts, and PSCFM, with enhanced OH − absorption and richer surface oxygen vacancies, is more inclined towards the Olattice-OOHcoupling. This work establishes a powerful ML paradigm and provides mechanistic insights, paving the way for accelerating the development of high-performance OER catalysts.

Material synthesis The PSCF, PSCFM and other catalysts were synthesized using a sol-gel method. As an example, the typical process for synthesizing PSCF is detailed as follows: 0.2 mmol of Pr(NO₃)3·6H₂O, 1.8 mmol of Sr(NO₃)2, 1 mmol of Co(NO₃)2·6H₂O, 1 mmol of Fe(NO₃)3·9H₂O and 4 mmol of CA were dissolved in 30 ml of H₂O. Then, 4 mmol of EDTA was slowly added. Finally, the NH₃·H₂O was dropwise added to adjust the pH value to 7–8. The beaker containing the solution was then placed on a heating platform at 90 °C with continuously stirring until a gel was formed. The beaker was then transferred to an oven at 200 °C for 10 h. Section 2 introduces the foundational components that underpin AI-driven MOF research, including curated data- bases, deep ML models and generative AI frameworks. Section 3 discusses AI-assisted material design and discovery workflows, highlighting forward design, inverse design, and active learning (AL) as key methodologies for navigating the vast MOF chemical space. Section 4 shifts the focus to AI-driven prediction and synthesis, where we detail recent progress in predicting intrinsic and functional properties, and guiding autonomous laboratory synthesis. Finally, Section 5 explores the application of AI- accelerated MOF development in diverse domains, including gas adsorption, separation, catalysis, water treatment, electronics, bio- medicine, and flame retardancy. By synthesizing insights across these topics, we aim to provide readers with a holistic under- standing of the opportunities, challenges, and emerging paradigms that AI brings to MOF research.

2.4 Hybrid AI-simulation strategies First-principles calculations have long served as foundational tools in computational materials science, including the study of MOFs. Among them, density functional theory (DFT) is widely used for electronic structure analysis, bandgap calcula- tions, adsorption site identification, and reaction mechanism elucidation. 88
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations capture the time-evolution of atomic interactions, offering insights into the thermal stability, mechanical properties, and dynamic behavior of MOFs under various conditions. 89 Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulations, on the other hand, are indispensable for evaluating adsorption isotherms and gas uptake capacities by simulating gas–solid equilibria under varying pressures and temperatures. 90 These methods, though powerful and physically grounded, are often computationally intensive, especially when applied to large-scale screening across thousands of hypothetical or experimental MOF structures. To overcome the limitations of scale and computational cost associated with first-principles simulations, recent efforts have focused on integrating these methods with ML and AI frame- works. For instance, in the large-scale screening of hypothetical MOFs, simulation-derived data, such as adsorption energies from GCMC or structural descriptors from DFT, are used to train surrogate ML models, enabling rapid property prediction across expansive chemical spaces. Alternatively, MD simulations can first generate reliable datasets, which are then modeled using regression techniques to accelerate the evaluation of previously unexplored structures. These hybrid approaches effectively com- bine the physical rigor of simulation with the scalability of AI, opening new avenues for data-driven, simulation-informed MOF design. Specific case studies will be discussed in subsequent sections.

3.1 Forward design High-throughput screening (HTS) originated from the concept of ‘‘combinatorial synthesis and testing of entire multicomponent systems’’ proposed in the 1970s, and was first widely adopted in drug discovery. Over the past decade, HTS has gained momen- tum in materials science, enabling the parallel assessment of vast MOF libraries to identify candidates with promising properties. 45
Current HTS strategies for MOFs typically follow a funnel-like workflow (Fig. 4(a)). 91 First, structural datasets are collected and preprocessed (as discussed in the previous sec- tion), and then a series of compounds is generated based on the predefined spatial structures and connectivity rules of the frame- works. Second, the dataset is filtered using structural descriptors such as pore diameter, surface area, and desolvation stability. Third, these geometrical and physical descriptors are combined with simulated properties or first-principles calculations to establish structure–property relationships. Based on the observed trends, a small subset of top-performing and experimentally promising MOFs is selected for further in-depth study or synthesis. 92 Several previous review articles have provided comprehensive summaries of HTS strategies. 91,93,94 Traditionally, high-throughput screening processes for MOFs have relied on computationally intensive simulations such as DFT and GCMC. While these first-principles methods provide high accuracy, their scalability is limited by the sub- stantial time and computational resources required, especially when applied to large structural libraries. To overcome these limitations, recent advances in deep ML and AI have been increasingly integrated into HTS workflows. Heuristic optimi- zation methods, including GNNs, genetic algorithms, and more recently, generative diffusion models, have been employed to enhance or even replace traditional simulation approaches. These data-driven models enable rapid prediction of key prop- erties, such as gas adsorption capacity, thermal conductivity, and structural stability, based on learned patterns, significantly accelerating the screening process.

Candidates with either high predicted values or high predictive uncertainty are preferentially selected. After each evaluation, the surrogate model is updated with the new structure–property data, and the cycle is repeated until structures with optimal properties and low uncertainty are discovered. This strategy has already been successfully applied in nano- porous materials discovery. For instance, Deshwal et al. employed BO to screen B70 000 hypothetical COFs for methane adsorption performance. 106 By substantially reducing the number of time-consuming GCMC simulations, BO rapidly identified top- performing candidates. Remarkably, the optimal COF was found after only 140 simulations, recovering B30% of the top-100 candidates, whereas random search required 500 simulations to identify only the 170th-ranked structure. These results highlight the superior efficiency of BO-driven AL compared with conven- tional random or evolutionary search strategies in accelerating materials discovery. AL has also been applied to MOF research, ranging from the optimization of synthesis conditions to accelerating computa- tional screening. For example, a robotic platform was employed to rapidly synthesize ZIF-67 via Joule heating, with two tunable chemical parameters (precursor volume and molar ratio) and two process parameters (applied voltage and reaction time). 107 Using the data generated by the robotic system, a BO algorithm iteratively proposed new synthesis conditions. As the iterations progressed, the crystallinity of the obtained ZIF-67 gradually improved, ultimately yielding the target crystalline phase while significantly reducing the number of screening experiments, reaction time, and energy consumption. Beyond synthesis, BO has been further developed for MOF design and property optimization. Rajabi-Kochi et al. introduced the feature-adaptive Bayesian optimization (FABO) framework, which systematically integrates feature selection into the BO loop. 108 By dynamically identifying the most influential descriptors during each optimization cycle, FABO enables efficient MOF discovery without requiring prior knowl- edge of key features. Using the QMOF and CoRE-2019 datasets, FABO successfully identified the top-performing MOFs for CO₂ adsorption and bandgap prediction within only 135 iterations, recovering over 20% of the top-100 candidates. Given the enormous design space of MOFs, exhaustive simulation or experimental evaluation is impractical. To address this, Comlek et al. proposed the latent variable Gaussian process with multi- objective batch Bayesian optimization (LVGP-MOBBO) frame- work (Fig. 5(b)). 109 Unlike conventional BO methods that rely on explicit physical descriptors, LVGP-MOBBO leverages quali- tative building-block representations to perform global optimi- zation. Remarkably, by exploring only B1% of the design space, the method successfully identified all Pareto-front solu- tions and over 97% of the top-50 candidates for CO₂ uptake and CO₂/N₂ selectivity. Compared with random forest models, LVGP demonstrated superior robustness and interpretability, as the latent variables provided physically meaningful insights into MOF design principles. A recent study by Dobbelaere et al. has pushed the boundary of AL for MOFs and developed a ‘‘cluster-based’’ learning methodology to build machine learning potentials (MLP) that accurately model spatial defects in large, disordered MOF systems comprising tens of thousands of atoms (Fig. 5(c) and (d)). 111 The key idea is to extract local chemical environ- ments as finite molecular fragments (‘‘clusters’’) from bulk MOF structures, feed them into MLP training, and selectively augment the training dataset where the model shows high uncertainty. By requiring significantly fewer ab initio reference data points, this AL-like workflow balances computational cost with accuracy, enabling the resultant potentials to reproduce the mechanical properties of disordered UiO-66-derived struc- tures with near-quantum mechanical fidelity. Recent advances in NLP and LLMs have further expanded the scope and efficiency of AL in MOF research by broadening the accessible initial datasets beyond curated databases to the vast body of scientific literature. 112 Early attempts relied on text- mining algorithms to autonomously extract feedback from exist- ing data; for instance, Nandy et al. employed NLP and image recognition to retrieve solvent stability and thermal degradation information for MOFs directly from experimental reports. 113 Subsequent studies extended this approach to the extraction of synthetic conditions from procedural texts, thereby enhancing the understanding of synthesis strategies. 55 More recently, LLMs have emerged as indispensable tools for literature-driven data mining, offering higher flexibility and accuracy than rule-based methods in parsing complex scientific knowledge. 114 Notably, Yaghi’s group introduced the GPT-4 Reticular Chemist framework, which performs MOF design and planning entirely through natural language interfaces without requiring coding, 87,115 while Kang and Kim’s ChatMOF integrated semantic retrieval from databases such as CoRE MOF and QMOF with generative modeling to predict properties and design novel MOFs with targeted function- alities (Fig. 5(e)). 56 When coupled with AL workflows, these LLM- enabled data extraction approaches not only expand the diversity of training datasets but also provide dynamic, literature-informed feedback loops, ultimately accelerating and refining the discovery of functional MOFs. AL offers a powerful paradigm shift for MOF discovery by introducing closed-loop, feedback-driven exploration that goes beyond conventional forward or inverse design strategies. This capability not only accelerates discovery but also expands the exploration space beyond established design heuristics, thereby fostering opportunities for uncovering unconventional MOF structures and properties. 116,117 Recent applications demon- strate the versatility of AL in addressing both experimental and computational challenges. 4.1 Prediction of intrinsic MOF properties In MOF synthesis and design, ML and AI enables the analysis of large datasets to reveal structure–property relationships and predict material performance. AI-guided prediction of MOF properties has not only enhanced research productivity but also signaled a transformative shift from traditional trial-and- error methods toward data-centric materials discovery. This evolution is instrumental in tackling critical global challenges across energy, sustainability, and healthcare sectors. Key intrin- sic properties, including band gap, band structure, and charge distribution, among others, as critical intrinsic characteristics of MOFs, play a pivotal role in their applications, such as gas adsorption, separation, and catalysis.
4.1.1 Structural feature prediction. The topological and
pore structures of MOFs are critical to their performance, particularly in adsorption and separation processes. ML models trained on large, curated databases can effectively extract mean- ingful patterns from ligand and metal node information to predict structural features and related performance metrics. For instance, Michael Fernandez et al. reported the first ML model that classifies the performance of MOFs using only simple geometric features, aiming to capture carbon from power plant flue gases. 118 Wang et al. trained an ML model using a filtered dataset of 9156 MOFs from the hMOF database, with hydrogen adsorption capacities calculated via GCMC simulations (Fig. 6(a)). 119 By integrating MOF geometric descriptors (e.g., pore size, surface area) with MOFid and MOFkey encoding schemes, they successfully developed a pre- dictive model for hydrogen storage performance. Furthermore, the development of generative artificial intel- ligence tools has expanded the application boundaries for predicting the structural features of MOFs, moving beyond conventional predictive models based on known data. For example, tools such as GHP-MOF-assemble have enabled the automatic creation of virtual MOF libraries and the prediction of key structural parameters like surface area and porosity. These tools can further screen for candidates with high CO₂ adsorption capacities (42 mmol g 1 ) through molecular dynamics simulations (Fig. 6(b)). 120 Together, these examples illustrate how data-driven ML and generative AI models can accelerate the discovery of functional MOFs by mapping the relationship between structure and performance, thereby enabling rapid screening and design of novel candidates.

4.2.2 Safety-related performance. AI-assisted prediction of
MOF functional properties has also extended into critical safety-related applications, such as flame retardancy and corro- sion resistance. These properties are inherently complex and difficult to quantify through conventional experiments alone due to their multivariate nature. AI offers advanced pattern recognition and multivariate analysis capabilities that enable precise modeling of nonlinear performance relationships. For instance, Zhang et al. demonstrates the power of AI/ML in accelerating the design of MOF-based polymeric nanocompo- sites by accurately predicting flame retardancy using a model trained on over 800 literature-derived data points. 141 Among five tested algorithms, the XGBoost model achieved the best performance (R² = 0.935), enabling experimental validation with only 6% prediction error and guiding further material optimization without the need for large-scale fire testing. In parallel, Anadebe et al. demonstrated the bifunctional role of Co-based MOFs as effective corrosion inhibitors for X65 steel in CO₂ environments, with strong agreement between experi- mental data and DFT/MD simulations, while an ANFIS model validates the predictive relationships for inhibition efficiency in practical pipeline protection (Fig. 7(i)–(k)). 142

By quantifying NBMO coefficients of organic ligands, the approach enables a symmetry-guided, data-informed framework that can be extended to machine-learning models for efficient discovery of spintronic MOFs with altermagnetic properties. Furthermore, a related theoretical study proposes a layer-mediated bilayer alter- magnet design strategy, demonstrating electric-field-tunable spin-splitting in bilayer MOFs through symmetry-guided screen- ing of spin point groups (Fig. 9(b)). 166 Very recently, Yue et al. developed a generalizable MLP for Zn-based MOFs using the data-efficient, equivariant nequIP architecture. 167 By train- ing on a curated dataset of DFT-augmented structures, the MLP accurately predicts forces, energies, and key physical properties across thousands of chemically diverse MOFs, which reduced the computational cost of high-throughput screening dramatically.

5.4 Catalysis AI and ML are transforming the development and refinement of MOF-based catalysts by facilitating data-driven innovations that surpass traditional empirical methods. Catalytic perfor- mance in MOFs depends heavily on active site structure (e.g., open metal centers, functionalized ligands, or embedded nano- particles), pore-mediated mass transport, and overall chemical stability. ML accelerates this process by extracting structure-
function relationships from large datasets and predicting opti- mal design configurations for specific catalytic reactions. For instance, Zhou et al. combined AI-based data mining with DFT calculations to reveal synergistic effects in multi- metallic MOFs, identifying Ni₃Fe₁-MOF as a superior oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst with an overpotential of just 208 mV (Fig. 12(a)). 181 This demonstrates how ML-guided screening can streamline multimetal catalyst discovery. Beyond OER catalysis, machine learning approaches have also been extensively applied to optimize MOF-based systems for carbon dioxide conversion. Li et al. employed multiple machines learning classifiers, including SVM, SGD, and neural networks, to predict the catalytic performance of MOFs in converting CO₂ to cyclic carbonates. 182 By training on experimental data and applying ensemble learning, they identified Mn, V, Cu, Ni, Zr,

Complementing such data-driven catalyst design, further research has focused on identifying underlying electronic and structural descriptors to enhance prediction interpretability and transferability. Mou et al. combined DFT calculations and machine learning to identify key descriptors—including metal intrinsic properties, con- strained coordination geometries, and linker electronic effects—for predicting CO₂ reduction performance on UiO-66-supported single- atom catalysts. 183 The models accurately predicted limiting poten- tials for C₁ products and demonstrated strong transferability to new functionalized systems, providing an efficient strategy for screening high-performance electrocatalysts. In photocatalysis, Bhavya Jaksani et al. integrated Bayesian optimization into a continuous-flow system for MOF-derived CuO/TiO₂ photocatalysts. 184 The AI model dynamically tuned reaction parameters in real time, increasing CO₂ conversion yield and achieving a record-breaking methanol production rate of 2.3 mol g 1 h 1, which is 2 to 100 times higher than those reported for batch processes. This highlights how ML enhances both material performance and process control. While real-time optimization significantly advances reaction efficiency, understanding the key factors governing photocata- lytic performance remains essential for rational catalyst and process design. Gheytanzadeh et al. employed GPR with multi- ple kernels to model tetracycline photocatalytic degradation over MOFs, identifying illumination time and surface area as the most critical parameters influencing efficiency, consistent with photochemical mechanisms. 185 The GPR-Matern model demonstrated superior prediction accuracy (R² = 0.981), provid- ing a robust computational framework for optimizing antibio- tic wastewater treatment processes. In biocatalysis, Chai et al. pioneered the use of random forest models to predict enzyme loading, immobilization effi- ciency, and reusability in enzyme@MOF composites, achieving R² = 0.85 and prediction errors below 25%. 186 This not only reduced experimental cost but also clarified the influence of key features like pore size and enzyme molecular weight, advancing AI-assisted design of robust biocatalytic systems. These examples highlight how AI/ML connects atomic-scale structures with catalytic performance across scales. To over- come current challenges like dynamic active site changes and solvation effects, future research will benefit from integrating ML with in situ characterization and multi-scale simulation for autonomous catalyst design.

5.7 Biological applications MOFs formed by metal nodes and biocompatible ligands, enable efficient drug delivery and multimodal therapies by combining high loading capacity, controlled release, and unique imaging properties into a single nanoscale platform. Recent progress leveraging ML for predicting biocompatibility and optimizing functional properties has significantly expanded MOF applications in tissue engineering, gene delivery, and intelligent diagnostics. MOFs’ high specific surface area, tunable pore sizes, and multifunctional surfaces enable breakthroughs in drug delivery, overcoming challenges like low drug loading capacity and poor targeting. Menon et al. developed an ML-driven high-throughput screening framework by integrating over 35 000 organic toxicity datasets to build an interpretable random forest model with 81% accuracy in toxicity classification (Fig. 13(b)–(d)).
194 By combining this with metal toxicity data (LD50), they screened 86 000 MOFs from the Cambridge Structural Database, identifying 479 low- toxicity candidates. This study reveals key chemical descriptors, such as carbonyl oxygen count and drug-likeness index that govern toxicity, and proposes a porosity-biocompatibility trade- off. This ML framework accelerates rational design by reducing experimental risks and shortening development cycles, offering valuable chemical insights for synthesizing safe, targeted drug delivery MOFs. ML-driven MOF design also enables breakthroughs in dis- ease diagnosis and therapy. For example, Kibria’s team con- structed a diabetes prediction model using Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms, enhanced by SHAP interpretability analysis, achieving a balanced accuracy of 90%, thus providing a reliable, transparent clinical decision support tool. 196 In cancer therapy, the integration of AI with MOFs enables a new generation of personalized and adaptive treatment strategies. 197 AI enhances drug delivery efficiency, targeting precision, and real-time response assessment by analyzing extensive datasets on tumor characteristics, patient responses, and MOF behavior at the nano- bio interface. ML models, including GAN-based virtual screening, facilitate the intelligent design of MOF-based theragnostic platforms, while future integration with organ-on-a-chip systems may further accelerate clinical translation. 198,199 This AI-driven approach allows dynamic optimization of treatment plans, mini- mizing side effects and maximizing therapeutic outcomes.
